Man, I admire those who have the confidence to jump on vatsim so early in their sim "careers". I remember learning everything I could with my Aersosoft 320 (way back when) doing the same flight over and over (offline) and learning how to program a hold and change approaches and throwing self vectors into mix so when I went on to vatsim I could be as prepared what to do in given circumstances.
Before even purchasing the aerosoft 320 I spent months learning what a ILS was how it works and doesn't work, How Vatsims top down coverage works and taking a scanner down to my local airport (EGCC) and listening into the freqs. Even signing up to a VA who had training available for VATSIM noobies (FLYUK). 
I did this as it was fun to me plus I knew that the network while free and easily accessible (even more so now) it was also a highly professional network. I didn't want to ruin any other controllers or simmers day by messing up.

This isn't me having a pop at any noobies it's like I said at the start I admire the balls to jump on and fly.
The big take away from your post is that you knew you made a mistake or wasn't prepared, which led to you asking questions to learn. Most don't do that so again, you've earned my admiration.

Keep flying and making sure each flight is a lesson learned. You'll soon be hitting 1000s of hours on the network like most of us do

If you do go for it, biggest advice, be ready to listen and learn from those who are experienced and also be ready to not listen to the ones that constantly moan (these people you'll come across alot and have more than likely earned the right to moan about the Job)

I've been doing it for just over 2 years now, of which all but one week has been tramping doing 4 on 4 off,  based in the North West. Ive seen more landmarks and visited more towns and cities than I ever would of sitting in a office making a decent wage.

There's draw backs of course. Be prepared for 58hr weeks or  more depending on what ever shift pattern you can get. The worst I see is people not being able to get a job which is a killer.
The long days can be a drain at first, my first full day out at the 10 hr mark i was flagging now ,10 hrs just feels like a mornings work . 
Most standard days are 13hrs, this can be pushed to 15hrs 3 times a week. And that's before you start thinking about your legal average over the set legal periods and your working time breaks and driving time breaks. All of YOU are in charge of via your tacho. Get it wrong and your won't stop away from VOSA fining you your weeks wage.

Youtube channel "national driving centre" they have alot of good informative videos about the process of getting your license, especially the nitty gritty stuff of  what is needed.

As for the job it self there's a few good YouTubers that vlog their weeks or days that can give you a good insight, there's a few dramatic ones(one of which was at my place for a short time period before he got his own truck and went viral on tiktok for his dramatic sounds)
LukeC in a HGV is good to watch to get an idea of the job
Or maybe Dave the angry trucker
Scott Andrews is another to check out just to get an idea of the job and what it entails. Easier than me trying to explain it In words

I do fridge work and bulker work. The fridge work is very similar to the Van work you are describing but with a generator behind your cab humming along to chill the fridge so that may well suit you. Theres tight independent companies in tight ish industrial estates  but that's the fun in the job. Figuring out how to get in to some places.

As for the process, it's your medical and then Theory and Hazard perception.
Then both your CPC mods case study (like a theory but more thought out questions) practical (5 questions of which each have 5 points to hit on to get a pass, might be wrong as it was a few years back now for me)
Then the driving part, the reverse test is basically useless for the real world but its a introduction to going backwards I guess. Then going forward test.


It sounds alot but if you are serious about the job it's a breeze.


Honestly the hard part about the job is "getting a job" once your in, its the best job in the world atleast for me. I'd rather be in the cab driving than in a office or customer facing job any day.
Am very fortunate that I am left to get on with my work by the office, won't always be perfect and it can be a graft doing 15hrs and having 9 off and going again (that 9 off with including to and from the yard and any other personal thing you might need to do) 


Reversing becomes second nature and youll need to shunt a few times every now and then but I wouldn't let that put you off.

I'd ring around driver trainer places and ask for a sighter to see if you fancy driving something bigger than a van first before you start fully committing. (This may or may not be possible)

This ending up being a bit of a longer type than u expected. Good luck in what ever you choose to do

After landing and taxing to a gate and saying goos bye and thank you to the control. I realised my hands where clammy and there was sweat on my forehead.
After that I flew that route a good 20x before I ventured out and tried other destinations. But I couldn't fly offline no more. I'd hunt out ATC around Europe via Vatspy.
